The fundamental principle of a criminal case in a trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and he is not required to prove his innocence by adducing evidence and that the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone. Even after the amendment of section 340 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by way of insertion of Sub-section (3) in sec-tion 340 of the said Code, by Ordinance No. XLIX of 1978, such presumption has not been changed altogether. After such amendment, any accused person of an offence before a criminal court shall be a competent witness for the defence and may give evidence on oath in disproof of the charge made against him. A proviso has been added in sub-section (3). Wherein it has been provided that the accused shall not be called as a witness except on his own request in writing and that his failure to give evidence shall not give rise to any presumption against him. The proviso clearly saves the accused from proving his innocence and that no adverse presumption can be drawn against the accused on his failure to give evidence in support of his defence. The intention of the Legislature for inserting such Provision enabling the accused to adduce evidence on oath, in our opinion, is to prove the plea of alibi specifically set up by the accused for absolving him from criminal liability particularly when the wife has been killed in the house of the husband or vice versa.
